text: RICOCHET combines client protection, server analytics, investigations, mitigations, and account security.
Activision’s internally developed kernel driver reports applications attempting to interact with protected games.
Activision says the driver installs automatically, starts with the game, and stops on game exit.
The FAQ requires the driver for protected PC games, without an opt-out.
The stated purpose is detecting game manipulation; no field-level telemetry schema is provided.
Protected PC titles listed: MW4, BO7, BO6, Warzone, MWIII, MWII, and Vanguard.
Activision reports stability testing across varied PCs and ongoing iteration, without quantitative failure rates.
RICOCHET was announced October 13, 2021, with backend protections for Vanguard and Warzone and a Warzone-first PC-driver rollout.
The driver was announced for PC; console players benefit from reduced PC cheating in cross-play, without receiving that Windows driver.
The launch promise was game-only operation and monitoring/reporting activity related to Call of Duty. This is a vendor commitment, not independent verification.
The original announcement already described ML examining server gameplay data for suspicious behavioral trends.
The December 7 announcement scheduled the driver rollout to begin in Asia-Pacific with Pacific launch, before worldwide expansion.
The December 15 progress report announced global PC-driver deployment, installed through the game update.
Damage Shield reduces a detected cheater’s ability to inflict lethal/critical damage while leaving that player vulnerable and available for investigation.
Damage Shield is described as a server-triggered response to detected tampering, not a mechanism for balancing ordinary players’ skill.
Extreme/repeated violations and attempts to disguise identity or hardware identity may result in permanent suspensions across accounts/titles.
Vanguard’s kernel driver launched globally April 26, 2022; upgrades were staged there before bringing Warzone’s driver to parity.
Cloaking hides legitimate opponents, including their relevant visual/audio cues, from detected cheaters while opponents can still see them.
Activision described both daily bans and ban waves; a single fixed ban cadence is not supported.
The report says cheating bans remove the offending player from the relevant leaderboards.
The team spans security, game/server engineering, research, and data science and collaborates with game-development teams.
Mitigations constrain detected cheaters while allowing collection and analysis; bans remain a separate enforcement outcome.
Disarm removes a detected cheater’s weapons, including fists.
Some damage still registers to preserve hit feedback and indicate the attack’s origin to the protected player.
Player reports help identify cheating trends and support investigations; the Q&A does not publish report-count thresholds.
locator: What can I do to help

text: The team identifies stolen/replacement accounts as part of the cheating ecosystem and recommends two-factor authentication.
locator: What can I do to help

text: The unified security platform introduced with MWII was intended to improve detection, mitigation development, and update frequency.
Activision described moving selected processes toward server-side execution to retain authority over more gameplay systems.
Driver updates were described as improving prevention and feeding additional information into detection and mitigation systems.
The report scheduled the driver for MWII’s October 28 and Warzone 2.0’s November 16 launch dates, globally.
The beta used only part of the security stack; full mitigations were reserved for launch. Beta behavior need not match launch behavior.
RIT reconstructs completed matches from captured/stored gameplay data for internal review; it is not described as recording the player’s desktop.
The team said it automatically captured high-tier Ranked match data and suspicious-account data across multiplayer modes.
Reports can flag accounts for review through tools including RIT.
Detection of controller-passthrough devices used to gain advantages such as recoil reduction was announced as globally deployed across platforms.
The published device-response sequence began with warnings and could escalate to mitigations, suspensions, or bans for continued misuse.
The team may adjust SR for players repeatedly benefiting from banned cheating partners, even without detecting cheats on those partners’ own machines.
Hallucinations are decoy characters supplied to flagged players and hidden from legitimate players.
They can disrupt verified cheaters or test suspicious accounts; interaction with an otherwise unseen decoy provides a detection signal.
locator: As a Mitigation; As a Detection

text: The published live design cloned an active player’s movement and presented plausible player information to cheat tools.
Quicksand slowed/froze cheaters through connection delay and could alter inputs; it was decommissioned because the visual disruption could distract legitimate players.
Configurable decoys invert the usual detection race: cheats must distinguish fake entities while defenders can vary their behavior.
The paper reports that popular cheating techniques treated the decoys as real players; this is a specific research result, not universal detection coverage.
ML assists behavioral discovery, abnormal-account challenges, action prioritization, and replay triage. The report says ML systems do not issue bans.
locator: How Does TeamRICOCHET Use Machine Learning

text: The replay model flags suspicious behavior such as wallhacks/rage cheating and prioritizes review by the team.
locator: Machine Learning x Replay Investigation Tool

text: Splat can disable a confirmed cheater’s parachute or alter velocity so a small fall becomes fatal.
Activision says player reports alone do not activate Splat and it is reserved for verified cheaters.
The report describes identifying more than 110,000 accounts exposed through reused credentials in 2023 and resetting them to prevent misuse.

scope: BO6 launch / titles sharing the driver
text: The BO6 launch plan included an updated kernel driver, new aimbot/behavioral ML, and existing mitigations.
Activision reported roughly 10 matches before removal in Beta Weekend One versus 5 in Weekend Two; these are historical observed averages.
The report says 25% of bans occurred in an account’s first match and over 12,000 confirmed cheating accounts were stopped before entering matches.
The team described using recorded Call of Duty League play to model elite legitimate performance, alongside cheating examples.
Activision acknowledged cheating methods beyond ordinary kernel visibility, including dedicated hardware; kernel access alone was not presented as sufficient.
The vendor reported a peak of 4.4 million categorized data points per hour, used to flag anomalous play for human review.
The 50 multiplayer-win entry condition supplied match history for review; AFK and regional-ping checks targeted boosting/VPN abuse.
The team announced manual review of rename requests at Crimson rank and above and replay monitoring of top players.
Some detections first ran in monitoring/data-only mode before being enabled to flag accounts for action.
locator: Launch Details; Ranked Play Security Updates

text: The team acknowledged that its Season 01 integration, particularly Ranked Play, fell short despite the earlier launch results.
The December report explicitly describes kernel-driver detections aimed at blocking memory tampering.
The team expanded its replay-rendering farm and human clip-review capacity, with detections influencing review priority.
The report says account bans were occurring hourly; this describes enforcement operations at that time, not a published detection interval.
The driver upgrade was announced to improve driver security and encryption, alongside a new tampering-detection system; algorithms were not specified.
The update identifies behavioral models, account trust, and hardware identifiers as inputs for targeting repeat cheaters.
The team said it did not use IP-address bans because shared networks would create collateral impact.
Repeated submissions from one reporter against one target are counted as one report, according to the team.
Accounts regularly partying with a banned cheater are flagged for investigation, supporting action against boosting.
LMM separates suspicious accounts during investigation; placement does not establish cheating.
Examples of LMM triggers include changed behavior or improbable new-account performance; thresholds are undisclosed.
An LMM party member brings the party into that pool; unaffected accounts return to standard matchmaking after leaving.
Activision says spam reports add no information and can reduce reporter trust or incur penalties.
The team states it rolls back account action found unwarranted during system-accuracy examinations.
The announced SR correction system refunded recent losses to banned cheaters and could remove gains earned with them; initial lookback was two weeks.
The team announced extra verification on new platform-account links, with gameplay blocked on that platform if verification fails.
Video plus game data produces a suspicious-behavior probability score; the published workflow elevates it for human validation.
RIT’s main focus in this update was Ranked multiplayer/battle royale, prioritizing high-scoring suspicious clips for faster review.
Activision reported an average of four matches before new cheating accounts were banned; this does not measure all undetected cheating.
The team reported legal demands to device/script vendors and said cheating with such tools could receive permanent bans.
TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot integration began as a phased test with notifications; those settings were not yet mandatory during Season 05.

text: The vendor claims no in-game-quality impact from these startup checks; this is not a benchmark of the entire anti-cheat stack.
Activision explicitly described verification of critical PC security settings through Microsoft infrastructure as Remote Attestation.
TPM can appear enabled in local Windows tools yet fail remote attestation because of firmware compatibility.
Activision says most detected cheaters were banned directly; more than 55,000 were disrupted with mitigations during August before permanent bans.
The update describes vehicles exploding for selected detected cheaters and suppressing their weapon/vehicle damage during investigation.
In-game Limited Matchmaking status notifications were announced as live.
The beta required TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot; the report tied further Microsoft Azure remote-verification upgrades to the November 14 launch.
The team announced a new generation of ML detections trained using millions of BO6 gameplay hours.
Anti-cheat systems were to be adjusted dynamically during the beta, with the full set of upgrades reserved for launch.
locator: Online for the Black Ops 7 Beta

text: The Season 01 report extended the TPM 2.0/Secure Boot requirement to Warzone.
The wizard was announced for later in Season 01 to check configuration and provide compliance guidance.
Updated boosting/botting detection targeted both artificially progressed accounts and the accounts running the services.
The team announced stronger pre-match remote verification using Microsoft Azure Attestation, building on TPM/Secure Boot requirements.
The announced method analyzes input timing, consistency, and response patterns rather than relying only on plugged-in device identity.
The system seeks classes of machine-generated recoil/aim behavior, because device configurations can change and lack one universal signature.
The rollout initially targeted common configurations and was described as iterative; it did not claim immediate detection of every setup.
SMS 2FA began with new accounts and planned expansion to existing accounts without ownership of a COD title from the preceding two years.
Recent-game ownership and SMS requirements are evaluated separately per linked platform, so ownership on one platform does not exempt another.
The team announced warnings that failing attestation would limit future playlist access.
Season 04 expanded MAA enforcement: failed/incomplete attestation routes players into separate matchmaking with limited playlists.
The listed access was Nuketown 24/7 in BO7 and Battle Royale Casual in Warzone; noncompliant PCs could not match with compliant PCs or consoles.
A noncompliant party member can cause the party to receive failed-attestation messaging and adjusted matchmaking.
The team acknowledges hardware/firmware compatibility failures unrelated to intentional tampering; fixes can depend on hardware manufacturers.
The vendor reported nearly two-thirds returned without the offending scripts. This is a behavioral-change claim about that cohort, not overall detection accuracy.
locator: Temporary Bans Deter Repeated Device Use

text: The team described combined pressure on cheats, replacement/stolen accounts, evasion services, resellers, and operators through technical and legal measures.
The report claimed over 375 reseller operations disrupted, over 80 legal demands, and 31 primary vendors shut down; definitions/time windows differ from older reports.
The report says more than 70,000 new hardware bans were issued during the preceding month; it does not disclose the identifier algorithm.
Technical detections seek unauthorized game interaction while behavioral systems analyze play over time to inform investigation and enforcement.
BO7/Warzone noncompliance can restrict modes, including Ranked, and place players in separate pools.
MW4 requires TPM 2.0/Secure Boot for all online modes; noncompliance blocks online gameplay.
The official wizard listing is version 1.3.0, updated October 21, 2026, for configuration/compliance diagnosis.
locator: Call of Duty Secure Attestation Wizard

text: The support page associates enrollaik.exe/UAC approval with generating an authorization key and validating TPM settings.
The wizard distinguishes TPM/Secure Boot disabled, GPT/UEFI configuration, BIOS update, authorization-key, and TCG-event-log problems.
The guide lists Windows 10 22H2+ or Windows 11 and UEFI/GPT for the supported Secure Boot configuration.
The privacy policy permits monitoring/recording gameplay, communications, device activities, and programs running alongside a game under applicable terms.
That broad policy covers multiple Activision properties and anti-fraud/toxicity systems; it does not establish that the kernel driver itself records all listed categories.
Activision offers a security intake leading to its private HackerOne program for qualifying vulnerabilities; player cheating reports belong in the in-game report tool.
Active account sanctions follow the Activision account across linked devices; sanctions can include warnings, temporary/permanent bans, Ranked restrictions, and corrections.
Device bans are distinct from account bans, can cover multiple titles, can vary in duration, and are not eligible for appeal.
The current policy says players/parties may not earn progression in LMM, and status can later return to normal, recur, or escalate.
Unauthorized memory/content modifications, unsupported cheating peripherals, and identity/hardware spoofing are sanctionable under the policy.
The enforcement policy applies from MW2019 onward; that is broader than evidence of where a particular kernel driver was deployed.
Temporary bans and LMM cannot be appealed; permanent-ban reversal is described as limited to determined account compromise. Hardware-ban status is checked in-game.
The public page says appeal decisions are final and duplicate or alternate-channel submissions will not receive responses.
David Andrews identifies himself as the anti-cheat lead; his answers describe engineering, data, operations, investigations, red teaming, and reverse engineering of cheats.
The lead declines to disclose driver specifics and would consider an equivalent driverless security approach if feasible.
The lead says AI is not making enforcement decisions, and behavioral signals are assessed alongside technical detections, telemetry, and investigations.
Ban waves/delays can reduce feedback to cheat developers or disrupt vendors, while normal operations prioritize keeping cheaters out quickly.
DMA was a priority; the IOMMU answer discussed evaluation, not a universal requirement.
The lead acknowledges historical LMM loops and describes increased monitoring plus Ranked and hardware bans as relieving pressure on LMM.
The PC feature announcement describes server detections, TPM/Secure Boot, investigations, legal pressure, email verification, and 2FA as the launch protection approach.
User-mode applications have separate virtual address spaces and restricted access to OS memory; kernel code runs in the operating system’s privileged context.
Kernel drivers are not isolated from the kernel/other drivers in the way ordinary applications are; a driver fault can crash the OS.
PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx registers callbacks for process creation/exit, providing a documented mechanism for system-level process observation.
Registered process callbacks must be removed before driver unload. A documented lifecycle requirement is not evidence of RICOCHET’s exact cleanup code.
ObRegisterCallbacks supports callbacks for process/thread/desktop handle operations. It is a plausible protection primitive, not proof of RICOCHET’s handle policy.
The callback code must reside in an appropriately signed kernel image; callbacks must be unregistered before unload.
PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine notifies a registered driver when executable images such as DLLs/EXEs are mapped or loaded.
An image-load callback describes an event surface; its existence does not establish complete visibility into every possible memory modification.
IOCTLs can carry requests between user-mode applications and drivers or between drivers; private vendor codes need not be publicly documented.
User-mode DeviceIoControl requests are delivered as IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL. RICOCHET-specific command IDs/payload formats cannot be inferred from this general interface.
Microsoft’s policy generally requires new kernel drivers to be signed through its developer portal on Windows 10 1607+, with documented legacy exceptions.
Driver signing establishes a loading/trust condition; it does not mean the binary has no vulnerabilities or performs only benign actions.
Azure’s documented model validates endorsement-key/certificate evidence, then binds an attestation identity key to a trusted TPM.
TPM-backed boot measurements provide evidence for a relying party’s policy evaluation; an attested state depends on what that policy actually checks.
Azure can evaluate measured Secure Boot variables and complementary code-integrity/HVCI/secure-launch evidence; these are platform capabilities, not confirmed COD requirements.
The client collects a TPM quote and TCG boot logs, submits evidence, and receives an attestation token if verification/policy checks succeed.
The relying party validates the attestation token’s signature using service signing metadata before relying on the resulting claims.
Microsoft’s generic workflow includes Microsoft Entra authentication; public COD announcements do not document its exact client-authentication path.
Secure Boot checks trust in boot components; Trusted Boot verifies subsequent OS components; Measured Boot records evidence for later verification.
Boot integrity and a trustworthy startup are distinct from continuously proving every later application action is legitimate.
DMA-capable PCIe-class peripherals can access system memory without the CPU performing each read/write; ordinary process-handle visibility does not describe this path.
Windows Kernel DMA Protection uses an IOMMU and device/driver remapping policy to restrict peripheral memory access.
The documented Windows feature needs supporting firmware, does not require VBS, and does not protect the pre-OS boot period.
Microsoft distinguishes device-specific DMA remapping from the overall Kernel DMA Protection policy; an enabled checkbox is not universal protection against all DMA threats.
VBS uses the Windows hypervisor for isolation; HVCI/Memory Integrity runs kernel code-integrity enforcement in that isolated environment.
HVCI restricts executable kernel pages and writable/executable combinations. It is a separate protection from TPM, Secure Boot, or a game’s kernel driver.
Microsoft documents attackers abusing legitimate signed drivers with vulnerabilities; signed code can still create kernel compromise risk.
The vulnerable-driver blocklist is a mitigation, not a guarantee of blocking every vulnerable driver; compatibility affects deployment.
Customers can configure which evidence/claims permit token issuance. A sample Azure policy is not Activision’s undisclosed production policy.
Azure packages attestation claims in a signed JWT; signature verification provides authenticity/integrity rather than automatically encrypting the claims.
MmCopyMemory copies physical or virtual memory into a caller buffer. Physical mode excludes I/O space; virtual mode uses system or current-process address space.
MmCopyMemory may return partial results/errors. Merely importing it does not prove that a driver scans all memory or uses every supported mode.
ETW separates event providers, session controllers, and consumers; it supports real-time consumption and file logging.
ETW imports alone do not establish what event fields are emitted, whether they are uploaded, or whether a remote ML model consumes them.
The protocol distinguishes basic TPM and TPM-plus-VBS requests. Using Azure Attestation does not by itself prove a game deploys a VBS enclave.
The service issues a challenge, and relying-party data can contain a nonce to bind evidence to a fresh attestation request.
Microsoft documents AIK certificate/public key, boot logs, and current/boot claims among attestation evidence; RICOCHET’s precise selection is not published here.
AMD documents fTPM 3.*.0.* attestation errors, fixed through firmware delivered to board manufacturers; the bulletin directs users to their motherboard vendor.
AMD notes TPM firmware updates can affect BitLocker recovery; firmware changes should follow the board vendor’s instructions and recovery-key guidance.
The August FAQ explicitly describes the kernel driver monitoring during gameplay and blocking tampering; boot protections complement rather than replace it.
Activision says uninstalling the protected game removes the driver; reinstalling includes it again.
SteamDB’s own detection rules associate the filename Randgrid.sys with Ricochet. A filename alone cannot establish a sample’s authenticity, version, or behavior.
The Valkyrie author reports an obfuscated Randgrid kernel driver with process-create notifications, memory-copy routines, and code-integrity checks identified through static analysis.
Reported imports include object callbacks, image notifications, ETW/WMI, cryptography, and firmware functions; import presence is not demonstrated execution of every proposed detection.
The report claims 688 imports, 329 VM opcodes, 63+ IOCTL commands, and about 1,058 signature entries. These counts were not independently reproduced here.
The reviewed README lacks a driver sample hash/precise game build, while some confidence labels rely only on imports; it is a research lead, not a current implementation specification.
The report discusses TPM-backed ActivisionAIK enrollment separately from kernel analysis. Official support corroborates the enrollment tool’s role but not every derived hardware-ban claim.
ssno’s first-hand article explicitly analyzes user-mode TAC in Black Ops Cold War; its hook/memory/obfuscation findings cannot simply be relabeled as RICOCHET kernel findings.
The cited ARES paper studies BattlEye, EAC, FACEIT, and Vanguard. Its rootkit-like-behavior results are not a RICOCHET test result.
CODUpdates acknowledged disabling a detection workaround that affected legitimate accounts and said affected accounts were restored. The post does not specify a kernel-level root cause.
Call of Duty announced new DMA-cheat detections launched ahead of DMZ Early Access that week. The visible official announcement does not disclose how detection works.
Call of Duty explains Server Culling as limiting opponent information sent to the client, reducing information available to wallhacks.
The official week-one post says suspected-cheating reports were trending below the prior year’s launch. The visible statement provides no quantitative detection/false-positive rate.
The whitepaper inserts fake entities while serializing server snapshots, before client processing, to avoid changing authoritative gameplay state.
Its chosen method copies a real-player snapshot entry into an unused entry and changes the copy; configurable generators update that decoy’s behavior.
The design must preserve plausible player data, conceal decoys from legitimate observation, remain maintainable/fast, and permit behavior changes.
Tests covered combinations of accessible features in three popular cheat programs; that finite test does not establish coverage of every present/future cheat.
The paper distinguishes deployed position/angle behaviors from an Emerge prototype and possible imitation-learning work; prototypes are not proof of current deployment.
The overview FAQ’s no-extra-driver-requirements wording does not override newer title-specific TPM/Secure Boot access rules.
August 2025’s optional test, December’s Warzone requirement, and June 2026’s restricted pools describe changing phases, not a single timeless access rule.
BO7/Warzone’s limited noncompliant access and MW4’s all-online restriction differ in the current support page; do not apply one title’s rule to all COD games.
A useful public-evidence model is pre-match trust checks plus runtime client/driver signals plus server behavior/replay investigation, followed by an appropriate response.
locator: Server vs Client; complementary systems; MAA

text: Published human validation of replay ML and statements that AI does not decide bans do not prove that a human individually approves every deterministic-rule ban.
locator: ML; RIT preview; AMA AI answer

text: Banned-account counts and time-to-action among detected cohorts do not reveal the total cheating population, recall, or false-positive rate.
Kernel privilege is not unlimited power over firmware, the hypervisor, TPM secrets, or remapped device memory; separate hardware/OS trust boundaries still matter.
Installed driver files/service registrations and a currently running driver are different lifecycle states.
